<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lemma:invariantalmostcomplexstructures}
Invariant almost complex structures on $\mathbb{F}_n$ are in one-to-one
correspondence with tournaments of order $n$.
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{std}
A finite digraph is balanced if and only if its set of arrows can be
partitioned into cycles.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By induction on the number of arrows. If there are no arrows, there is
nothing to prove. Otherwise, let $e_1$ be an arrow from $i_0$ to
$i_1$. Since the digraph is balanced, there is some arrow going out of
$i_1$, say $e_2$. This gives an infinite sequence $\{e_j\}$; because
the digraph is finite, at some point a vertex must be repeated, and
this gives a cycle.  Removing the cycle, one obtains another
balanced digraph, to which the induction hypothesis can be applied.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{circ}
Let $n\geqslant3$ be odd. The \emph{circulant tournament}, denoted in this
paper by $\mathscr{T}_n$, is the digraph in which $i\to j$ is an edge if and
only if $j-i\equiv 1,\ldots, (n-1)/2\pmod n$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{tacs}
The tournament associated to an invariant almost complex structure on
$\mathbb{F}_n$ is regular if and only if $\kappa$ is trivial.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The space $\Lambda^{1,0}$ of $(1,0)$-forms is a direct sum of the
lines $\overline{L_i}\otimes L_j$, so there is an isomorphism
\[\kappa\ \cong\ \bigotimes_{i\to j} \overline{L_i}\otimes L_j.\]
If $\mathscr{T}$ is regular, each occurrence of $L_i$ on the right-hand side
will be matched by an occurrence of $\overline{L_i}$ (and their
multiplicities will also be equal). Thus, the product is trivial.

Conversely, suppose that $\kappa$ is trivial. Treat $\overline{L_i}$ on the
right-hand side as $L_i^{-1}$. Each arrow has a head and a tail, so
the total number of negative powers must equal the total number of
positive powers. Now tensor the right hand side by a power of the
trivial tensor product
\[ \lambda=L_0\otimes\cdots\otimes L_{n-1}\cong\Lambda^n(\mathbb{C}^n)\]
so that only non-negative powers of all $L_i$ persist. Since the
product remains trivial, it must itself be a power of $\lambda$, as
such a power is the only trivial 1-dimensional representation of
$T^{n-1}$. It follows that the original product was (up to permutation
of factors) $\overline\lambda{}^{(n-1)/2}\otimes\lambda^{(n-1)/2}$, and the in-
and out-degrees are equal at every node.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{spin}
For any $n$, the full flag manifold $\mathbb{F}_n$ is spin.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
If $n$ is odd, $\mathbb{F}_n$ admits an invariant orthogonal almost complex
  structure with $\kappa$ trivial, equivalently an $\mathrm{SU}(N)$
  structure. The latter lifts to an inclusion $\mathrm{SU}(N)\to \mathrm{Spin}(2N)$.

If $n$ is even, we need to show that for some invariant almost complex
structure $\kappa$ admits a square root. Label the nodes
$0,1,2,\ldots,n-1$, and choose a regular tournament on the complete
subgraph $K_{n-1}$ generated by $1,\ldots, n-1$. Then add all the
directed edges $0\to k$ for $1\leqslant k\leqslant n-1$, so as to define a
so-called reducible tournament. In the regular tournament on
$\{1,\dots,n-1\}$ each vertex has equal in- and out-degree, so its
contribution $\bigotimes_k(\overline{L_k}\otimes L_k)^{(n-2)/2}$ to the
canonical bundle is trivial, and
  \[\kappa \cong \overline{L_0}^{\,n-1}\otimes L_1\otimes\cdots\otimes L_{n-1}\cong
  \overline{L_0}^{\,n-1}\otimes\overline{L_0}=\overline{L_0}^{\,n},\]
in which the middle isomorphism arises from the fact that
$L_0\otimes\cdots\otimes L_{n-1}=\Lambda^n(\mathbb{C}^n)$ is a trivial line
bundle. Thus $\kappa^{1/2}\cong \overline{L_0}^{\,n/2}$, which exists
because $n$ is even.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lemma:neven}
If $\mathbb{F}_n$ has nonzero invariant spinors, then $n$ is odd.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Fix an invariant almost complex structure associated to a tournament $\mathscr{T}$; a spinor is a section of $\kappa^{1/2}\otimes\Lambda^{0,\bullet}$. As a representation of $\mathfrak{t}^n$, $\Lambda^{0,\bullet}$ decomposes into
the direct sum of $1$-dimensional representations, each corresponding to a decomposable form in some $\Lambda^{0,q}$. Accordingly, an invariant spinor is a linear combination of invariant elements of the form $\epsilon\otimes\psi_\mathscr{U}$, where $\epsilon$ is a generator of $\kappa^{1/2}$ and $\mathscr{U}$ varies among subgraphs of $\mathscr{T}$, balanced or not. The square of $\epsilon\otimes\psi_\mathscr{U}$ effectively belongs to
\[\bigotimes_{i\to j \text{ in } \mathscr{T}\setminus\mathscr{U}} \overline L_i\otimes L_j \otimes \bigotimes_{i\to j\text{ in } \mathscr{U}}\overline{L_j}\otimes L_i,\]
which is the canonical bundle of the almost complex structure obtained by reversing the arrows of $\mathscr{T}$ contained in $\mathscr{U}$. Arguing as in Lemma~\ref{tacs}, the fact that this canonical bundle is trivial implies that the in-degree and out-degree coincide at each vertex, which is only possible if $n$ is odd.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lemma:basis}
If $\mathscr{U}$ is a balanced subgraph, $\psi_\mathscr{U}$ is invariant; the $\psi_\mathscr{U}$ thus obtained form a basis of the space of invariant spinors.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
The argument of Lemma~\ref{tacs} shows that invariance of $\psi_\mathscr{U}$ is equivalent to $\mathscr{U}$ being balanced; that this gives a basis follows from the fact that each $\psi_\mathscr{U}$ spans  a $1$-dimensional representation of $\Lambda^{0,\bullet}$.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lemma:pure}
If $\mathscr{U}$ is a balanced subgraph, $\psi_\mathscr{U}$ is invariant and pure; the almost complex structure defined by $\psi_\mathscr{U}$ is regular, and corresponds to the tournament  $\mathscr{T}_n\mathbin{\oslash} \mathscr{U}$ obtained from $\mathscr{T}_n$ by reversing the arrows of $\mathscr{U}$.
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Given $\mathscr{U}$, we compute the space
\[V=\{v\mid v\cdot\psi_\mathscr{U}=0\}.\]
It is clear that
\begin{equation*}
\begin{split}
\overline\alpha_{ij}\cdot\psi_\mathscr{U}&=\sqrt2\overline\alpha_{ij}\wedge \psi_\mathscr{U}=0 \text{ if $i\to j$ in $\mathscr{U}$}\\
 \alpha_{ij}\cdot\psi_\mathscr{U}&=-\sqrt2\alpha_{ij}\lrcorner\, \psi_\mathscr{U}=0 \text{ if $i\to j$ is not in $\mathscr{U}$}
 \end{split}
\end{equation*}
Thus, $V$ has maximal dimension and $\psi_\mathscr{U}$ is pure. Its space of
$(1,0)$-vectors is obtained from the space of $(1,0)$-vectors for the
almost complex structure defined by $\mathscr{T}_n$ by conjugating the
components corresponding to elements of $\mathscr{U}$. In particular the
canonical bundle is generated by
\begin{equation}\label{wedge}
  \prod_{i\to j\in\mathscr{U}} \overline\alpha_{ij}\;\;\hbox{\large$\wedge$}\kern-8pt
  \prod_{i\to j\in\mathscr{T}_n\setminus \mathscr{U}} \alpha_{ij}.
\end{equation}
Arguing as in Lemma~\ref{tacs}, we see that both factors are
invariant, hence $\kappa$ is invariant and the almost complex
structure defined by $\psi_\mathscr{U}$ is regular. Thus, it is the almost
complex structure defined by a regular tournament, which by construction is $\mathscr{T}_n\mathbin{\oslash} \mathscr{U}$.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lemma:trivialcanonicalbundle}
The almost complex structure defined by a pure invariant spinor is regular.
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
By \cite[III.3.2]{Chevalley_1996}, we have a squaring map
\[\Delta \otimes\Delta\to\Lambda^{\bullet}\otimes \Lambda^{0,N},\]
with $\Lambda^\bullet$ denoting the complexified exterior algebra; if $V$ is the maximal isotropic space determined by a spinor $\psi$,
the image of $\psi\otimes \psi$ lies in $\det
V\otimes\Lambda^{0,N}$. Since $\psi\otimes\psi$ is invariant and
$\Lambda^{0,N}=\overline\kappa$ is trivial (the reference structure $\mathscr{T}_n$
being regular), this implies that $\det V$ is also trivial, i.e. the
almost complex structure defined by $\psi$ has trivial canonical
bundle.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{akin}

The number of balanced subgraphs of a regular tournament of order $n$
is precisely $\mathrm{RT}(n)$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Fix a regular tournament $\mathscr{T}$. Lemma~\ref{lemma:pure}, Lemma~\ref{lemma:trivialcanonicalbundle} and
Lemmas~\ref{lemma:invariantalmostcomplexstructures}, \ref{tacs} (in
this order) determine maps $f,g,h$ that fit in the following
commutative diagram:
\[\xymatrix{\{\text{balanced subgraphs of } \mathscr{T}\}\ar[r]\ar[d]^f & \{\text{regular tournaments on the $n$ nodes}\}\ar[d]^{h}\\
 \{\text{pure invariant spinors}\}/\mathbb{C}^* \ar[r]^g&
  \left\{\parbox{3cm}{\centering regular invariant\\ almost complex structures}\right\}
 }
\]
In this diagram, $f$ is injective and $h$ is a bijection; the map $g$ is a special case of the correspondence between almost complex structures and pure spinors, hence also a bijection. Furthermore, the argument leading to Lemma~\ref{lemma:invariantalmostcomplexstructures} shows that every invariant almost complex structure is obtained from the fixed one by reversing the arrows of a subgraph; by Lemma~\ref{tacs} the resulting structure is regular precisely when the subgraph is balanced. Thus $g\circ f$ is surjective, and all the arrows in the diagram are bijections.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:dim}
The dimension of the space of invariant spinors $\Xi_n$ on $\mathbb{F}_n$ is $\mathrm{RT}(n)$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{Pd}
  $\dim\Xi_{n,q}=\dim\Xi_{n,N-q}$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
If $\mathscr{S}$ is a balanced subgraph of $\mathscr{T}$,
    so is its complement $\mathscr{T}\setminus\mathscr{S}$, and this establishes an
    isomorphism $*\colon\Xi_{n,q}\to\Xi_{n,N-q}$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The image of $t_j$ in $\mathrm{O}(2N)$ reverses orientation, since it compounds $2n-3$ reflections.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:cliffordcovers}
By construction, $\hat\Sigma_n$ acts linearly on $\Xi_n$.
Relative to $\Sigma_n$, $\Xi_n$ is only a projective representation. It is known (see \cite[Theorems 2.9 and 2.12]{Hoffman_Humphreys_1992}) that all projective representations of $\Sigma_n$ can be lifted to linear representations of one of its Schur covers. For $n\geq 4$, $\Sigma_n$ has two Schur covers $\tilde\Sigma_n$ and $\hat\Sigma_n$, distinguished by whether transpositions lift to elements of order four or two; $\Sigma_3$ is its own Schur cover, but we will extend the definitions to $n=3$ for a uniform treatment. Both $\tilde\Sigma_n$ and $\hat\Sigma_n$ can be realized  inside the complex Clifford algebra of $\mathbb{R}^n$, taking $-1$ and either
\[\frac 1{\sqrt2}(e_j-e_{j+1}), \frac i{\sqrt2}(e_j-e_{j+1})\]
as generators; under twisted conjugation, both act as $\Sigma_n$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$. A complex spin representation of either group induces a representation of the other by letting e.g. $\frac i{\sqrt2}(e_j-e_{j+1})$ act as $i$ times the action of $\frac 1{\sqrt2}(e_j-e_{j+1})$.

In this description, the intersection of $\tilde\Sigma_n$ and $\hat\Sigma_n$ is the $2:1$ cover of the group of even permutations, and in this intersection two representations in the above correspondence coincide.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lemma:oddlift}
If $\sigma$ has odd order $d$ in $\Sigma_n$, then it lifts to a unique element $\tilde \sigma$ of odd order in $\hat\Sigma_n$; the order of $\tilde\sigma$ is $d$.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
There are two elements in $\hat\Sigma_n$ covering $\sigma$, say $\tilde \sigma$ and $z\tilde \sigma$. Each has necessarily order $d$ or $2d$. Since $d$ is odd,
\[(z\tilde \sigma)^d = z^d\tilde \sigma^d=z \tilde\sigma^d;\]
thus, exactly one has order $d$.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The unique lift with odd order of a permutation with only odd cycles is the product of the odd lifts of each cycle, which commute.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lemma:edgecycles}
Let $\sigma$ be a permutation in $\Sigma_n$ that only has odd cycles. The cycles of $\rho(\sigma)$ are determined  as follows:
\begin{enumerate}
\item two distinct cycles of lengths $a$ and $b$ contribute $\gcd(a,b)$ cycles of length $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)$, formed by the edges joining them;
\item a cycle of odd length $a$ contributes $(a-1)/2$ cycles of length $a$, formed by the edges joining its nodes.
\end{enumerate}
In particular, $\rho(\sigma)$ only has odd cycles.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $A$ and $B$ be distinct cycles of $\sigma$, of lengths $a$ and $b$. An edge joining a node of $A$ to a node of $B$ is mapped by $\rho(\sigma)$ and each power $\rho(\sigma)^k$ to an edge of the same form; since the endpoints cannot be interchanged, the edge returns to itself when both endpoints do, i.e. when $k$ is a multiple of $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)$. Hence the $ab$ edges joining $A$ to $B$ split into $\gcd(a,b)$ cycles of $\rho(\sigma)$, each of length $\operatorname{lcm}(a,b)$.

For the edges with both endpoints in a single cycle $A$ of length $a$, identify $A$ with $\mathbb{Z}/a\mathbb{Z}$ so that $\sigma$ acts as $x\mapsto x+1$; an edge is then a pair $\{x,x+d\}$, and the edges
\[\{x,x+d\}, \dotsc, \{x+(a-1),x+(a-1)+d\}\]
are distinct because $a$ is odd.

The final statement follows trivially.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:trace}
Let $\sigma$ be a permutation in $\Sigma_n$.
\begin{itemize}
 \item if $\sigma$ contains even cycles and $\tilde\sigma$ is any lift to $\hat\Sigma_n$, $\operatorname{tr} (\tilde \sigma|_{\Xi_n})=0$;
 \item if $\sigma$ only contains odd cycles, then its odd-order lift  satisfies $\operatorname{tr} (\tilde \sigma|_{\Xi_n})=\left\vertT_\sigma\right\vert$.
 \end{itemize}
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
We compute the trace by evaluating on the basis of pure invariant spinors. If $\psi$ is pure and invariant, then so is $\tilde\sigma(\psi)$, and $\psi$ only gives a contribution to the trace of $\tilde\sigma$ if $\tilde\sigma(\psi)=c\psi$ for some complex scalar $c$; this means that $\tilde\sigma(\psi)$ determines the same almost complex structure as $\psi$, or  equivalently the same regular tournament.  Thus, we only need to consider pairs $(\sigma,\psi)$ such that the regular tournament associated to $\psi$ is in $T_\sigma$. In particular, $\sigma$ only has odd cycles, hence odd order $d$; by Lemma~\ref{lemma:oddlift}, it has a unique odd-order lift $\tilde\sigma$, whose order is also $d$.

Fix a tournament in $T_\sigma$, with associated pure spinor $\psi$, and use the corresponding almost complex structure to identify spinors with $\Lambda^{0,\bullet}$, so that $\psi=1$. Let $W$ be the real span of the products of the $\overline{\alpha_{ij}}$ with $i\to j$ in this tournament, so that $\Lambda^{0,\bullet}=W\oplus iW$; Clifford multiplication by each $\alpha_{ij}$ maps $W$ to itself. Expanding the generators $t_j$, we see that $t_j\cdot W\subset iW$, because $n-2$ is odd. Since $\sigma$ is an even permutation, $\tilde\sigma$ is a product of an even number of generators up to sign, so $\tilde\sigma\cdot W\subset W$ and $c$ is real. Then  $\psi=\tilde\sigma^d(\psi)=c^d\psi$ forces $c=1$, because $d$ is odd; thus, each element of $T_\sigma$ contributes $1$ to the trace.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lemma:count}
Let $\sigma$ be a permutation in $\Sigma_n$ whose cycles have odd lengths $a_1,\dotsc, a_m$, and set $g_{ij}=\gcd(a_i,a_j)$, $L=\sum_i (a_i-1)/2$. Then
\[\left\vertT_\sigma\right\vert=2^{L}\bigl[y_1^{(n-a_1)/2}\cdots y_m^{(n-a_m)/2}\bigr]\prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant m}\Bigl(y_i^{a_j/g_{ij}}+y_j^{a_i/g_{ij}}\Bigr)^{g_{ij}}.\]
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Write $A_1,\dotsc, A_m$ for the cycles of $\sigma$, viewed as subsets of the set of nodes. Since all the $a_i$ are odd, the proof of Lemma~\ref{lemma:edgecycles} shows that whenever a power of $\sigma$ maps an edge to itself, it fixes both endpoints; hence every $\rho(\sigma)$-orbit of edges can be directed $\sigma$-equivariantly, in exactly two ways, each determined by the direction of any single edge in the orbit. The $\sigma$-invariant tournaments are obtained by directing each orbit independently, and we must count the choices for which the resulting tournament is regular.

By the first item in Lemma~\ref{lemma:edgecycles}, nodes of distinct $A_i$ and $A_j$ are connected by $g_{ij}$ edge orbits, each containing $a_ia_j/g_{ij}$ edges. For each edge orbit, assigning the direction from $A_i$ to $A_j$ contributes $a_j/g_{ij}$ to the out-degree of each node of $A_i$. Thus, the choice corresponds to the generating function $y_i^{a_j/g_{ij}}+y_j^{a_i/g_{ij}}$ in the polynomial ring $\mathbb{R}[y_1,\dotsc, y_m]$. Since there are $g_{ij}$ independent choices for every $i<j$, the overall generating function is
\[
 \prod_{1\leqslant i<j\leqslant m}\Bigl(y_i^{a_j/g_{ij}}+y_j^{a_i/g_{ij}}\Bigr)^{g_{ij}},\]
where the coefficient of $y_1^{e_1}\cdots y_m^{e_m}$ counts choices contributing $e_i$ to the out-degree of nodes of $A_i$.

By the second item of Lemma~\ref{lemma:edgecycles}, the edges connecting nodes of a fixed $A_i$ form $(a_i-1)/2$ orbits,  giving $2^{(a_i-1)/2}$ choices. Each choice amounts to fixing a $\mathbb{Z}/a_i\mathbb{Z}$-invariant tournament on $\mathbb{Z}/a_i\mathbb{Z}$, which is necessarily regular, i.e. the out-degree of each node is $(a_i-1)/2$. The generating function is therefore $2^{(a_i-1)/2} y_i^{(a_i-1)/2}$; taking the product and extracting the coefficient of $y_1^{(n-1)/2}\dotsm y_m^{(n-1)/2}$ gives a formula equivalent to the one in the statement.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:count}
For the $n$-cycle, Lemma~\ref{lemma:count} trivially gives $\left\vertT_\sigma\right\vert=2^{(n-1)/2}$.

The class $(3^3)$ at $n=9$ exercises the method at full strength: since $g_{ij}=3$ and $a_j/g_{ij}=1$ for all $i,j$, Lemma~\ref{lemma:count} reads
\[\left\vertT_\sigma\right\vert=2^3\,\bigl[y_1^3y_2^3y_3^3\bigr]\,(y_1+y_2)^3(y_1+y_3)^3(y_2+y_3)^3.\]
Expanding powers into monomials, each monomial of $(y_1+y_2)^3$ only gives a contribution if paired with fixed choices in the expansion of the other two factors, leading to
\[\bigl[y_1^3y_2^3y_3^3\bigr]\,(y_1+y_2)^3(y_1+y_3)^3(y_2+y_3)^3
=\sum_{k=0}^3\binom3k^3=56,\]
so $\left\vertT_\sigma\right\vert=2^3\cdot56=448$, matching Table~\ref{tab:support}.

Similarly, for $(5^2,3)$ at $n=13$,
\[\left\vertT_\sigma\right\vert=2^5\,\bigl[y_1^4y_2^4y_3^5\bigr]\,(y_1+y_2)^5(y_1^3+y_3^5)(y_2^3+y_3^5)=
2^5\biggl(\binom51+\binom54\biggr)=320.\]
For $(3,1^2)$ at $n=5$, $T_\sigma$ is empty, because
\[[y_1 y_2^2y_3^2] (y_1+y_2^3)(y_1+y_3^3)(y_2+y_3)=0.\]
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:multiplicity}
For every strict partition $\lambda$ of $n$,
\[
m_\lambda=\sum_{\rho}\frac{\left\vertT_\rho\right\vert}{z_\rho}\,\overline{\chi_\lambda(\rho)},
\]
where $\rho$ ranges over partitions of $n$ into odd parts and $\chi_\lambda(\rho)$ denotes the value of $\chi_\lambda$ on the odd-order lift of a permutation of cycle type $\rho$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The standard projection formula can be written as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:multiplicities}
  m_\lambda \;=\;
  \frac1{\left\vert\hat\Sigma_n\right\vert}\sum_{\tilde\sigma\in\hat\Sigma_n}
  \chi_{\Xi_n}(\tilde\sigma) \overline{\chi_\lambda(\tilde\sigma)}.
\end{equation}
Since $\chi_{\Xi_n}(\tilde\sigma)\overline{\chi_\lambda(\tilde\sigma)}=
  \chi_{\Xi_n}(z\tilde\sigma)\overline{\chi_\lambda(z\tilde\sigma)}$, we have
\[
 m_\lambda \;=\;
  \frac1{\left\vert\Sigma_n\right\vert}\sum_{\sigma\in\Sigma_n}
  \chi_{\Xi_n}(\tilde\sigma)\overline{\chi_\lambda(\tilde\sigma)}.
\]
By Proposition~\ref{prop:trace}, the only $\tilde\sigma$ contributing to the sum are those projecting to permutations that decompose into odd cycles; choosing the odd-order lift gives the formula in the statement.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- example-2: body_md -->
For $n=3$,  both regular tournaments
of order three are invariant under a $3$-cycle, so
$\left\vertT_{(3)}\right\vert=\left\vertT_{(1^3)}\right\vert=2$, and Corollary~\ref{cor:multiplicity} gives
\[m_{(3)}=\tfrac26\cdot2+\tfrac23(-1)=0,\qquad
m_{(2,1)^\pm}=\tfrac26+\tfrac23=1.\]
For $n=5$ only $\rho=(5)$ and $\rho=(1^5)$ have $\left\vertT_\rho\right\vert\ne0$ (see Example~\ref{ex:count});
the values of Table~\ref{tab:spinchar} give
\[m_{(3,2)}=m_{(5)}=\frac{24}{120} \cdot 4 + \frac45(-1)=0,\quad
m_{(4,1)}=\frac{24}{120}\cdot6+\frac45\cdot1=2.
\]
For $7\leqslant n\leqslant13$, every spin representation occurs (see Table~\ref{tab:decomp} below).
<!-- end example-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
Let $\lambda$ be a strict partition of $n$ with $\ell$ parts, and write
$k=n-\ell$. Suppose that, modulo eight,
\[n\equiv 1,3\ \text{ and }\ k\equiv 4,5,6,\qquad\text{or}\qquad
n\equiv 5,7\ \text{ and }\ k\equiv 0,1,2.\]
Then $m_\lambda$ is even.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
It is a general fact that the multiplicity of a representation $V$ in
$W$ is even if one of $V,W$ is real and the other quaternionic,
because $V^*\otimes W$ is quaternionic.

By Schur \cite[Satz III]{Schur_1927} the representation
labelled $\lambda$ is of real type when $k\equiv 0,1,2\pmod 8$, of complex
type when $k\equiv 3,7$, and of quaternionic type when $k\equiv 4,5,6$.

On the other hand, the spinor representation $\Delta$ is real when
$2N\equiv 0,6\pmod 8$ and quaternionic when $2N\equiv 2,4$; the
actions of $T^n\subset\mathrm{Spin}(2N)$ and $\hat\Sigma_n\subset \mathrm{Pin}(2N)$
preserve the structure, hence $\Xi_n$ is a
$\hat\Sigma_n$-representation of real type when $n\equiv 1,3\pmod 8$
and of quaternionic type when $n\equiv 5,7$. The statement follows.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:eigenspinors}
$\Xi_n$ splits as the sum of two eigenspaces for $D$ with eigenvalue
$\pm\frac14\sqrt{3n(n^2-1)}$, each of
dimension $\tfrac12\mathrm{RT}(n)$.
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
Since $D$ interchanges chirality, $\operatorname{tr} D=0$; it is therefore sufficient to show that
\begin{equation}
\label{eqn:squareD}
D^2=\frac{3n(n^2-1)}{16}\,\operatorname{Id}.
\end{equation}
Since $\Xi_n$ is generated by pure spinors, it suffices to compute $D^2\psi$ for $\psi$ pure. We can use the complex structure defined by $\psi$ itself, so that $\psi=1$ as a form. Then
\[D\psi=\frac1{\sqrt2}\sum_{i,j,l}\alpha_{ij}\wedge \alpha_{jl}\wedge \alpha_{li},\]
where the sum is over $i,j,l$ such that $\alpha_{ij}$, $\alpha_{jl}$, $\alpha_{li}$ have type $(0,1)$; equivalently, over cycles $jil$ in the tournament $\mathscr{T}$ defining the fixed complex structure.

The operator $D$ has odd degree, and being cubic, $D^2$ can only change the degree by $0,2,4,6$ (only raising occurs, since $\psi=1$); however, $D^2\psi$ cannot have components of degree two, because there are no balanced subgraphs with two edges. Moreover  $D^2\psi$ has no component of degree six, because three-forms anticommute. Degree four components in $D^2\psi$ arise from terms
\[\alpha_{ik}\wedge\alpha_{kj}\wedge \alpha_{ji}\lrcorner\, (\alpha_{ij}\wedge \alpha_{jl}\wedge \alpha_{li})=-\alpha_{ik}\wedge\alpha_{kj}\wedge \alpha_{jl}\wedge \alpha_{li} \]
where $jil$ and $kilj$ are directed cycles in $\mathscr{T}$. In other words,
this degree $4$ spinor is obtained by joining a directed $3$-cycle in
$\mathscr{T}$ and one that has an inverted arrow compared to the tournament,
with the two differently oriented arrows `canceling out'.

Now whenever  $jil$ and $kilj$ are directed cycles,  $\mathscr{T}$ contains
either $kil$ or $klj$, and we obtain corresponding terms
\begin{align*}
\alpha_{kj}\wedge\alpha_{jl}\wedge \alpha_{lk}\lrcorner\, (\alpha_{ik}\wedge \alpha_{kl}\wedge \alpha_{li})&=\alpha_{kj}\wedge\alpha_{jl}\wedge \alpha_{ik}\wedge  \alpha_{li},\\
\alpha_{li}\wedge\alpha_{ik}\wedge \alpha_{kl}\lrcorner\, (\alpha_{lk}\wedge \alpha_{kj}\wedge \alpha_{jl})&=-\alpha_{li}\wedge\alpha_{ik}\wedge \alpha_{kj}\wedge \alpha_{jl}.
\end{align*}
This amounts to dividing a square into two triangles by choosing a diagonal; the diagonal that is chosen determines the resulting sign, so the overall sum is zero.

Thus, the only surviving terms come from contracting a cycle with its
inverse, for example
\[\alpha_{ji}\cdot\alpha_{il}\cdot\alpha_{lj}\cdot\alpha_{ij}\cdot \alpha_{jl}\cdot\alpha_{li}\cdot 1=(-2\sqrt2 )(-2\sqrt2)=8;
\]
each $3$-cycle determines $9$ summands, because indices can be reordered. Since a regular tournament has $n(n^2-1)/24$ oriented $3$-cycles,
\[D^2\psi = \frac1{16} 72 \left\vert\{\text{oriented $3$-cycles}\}\right\vert =\frac92\frac{n(n^2-1)}{24}=\frac{3n(n^2-1)}{16}.\]
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:doubling}
The operator $A\colon\Xi_n\to\Xi_n$ commutes with the action of
$\hat\Sigma_n$ and satisfies $A^2=-\operatorname{Id}$. Its eigenspaces $P^+$ and
$P^-$ are subrepresentations, and
\[\Xi_n\cong P^+\oplus(P^+\otimes\operatorname{sign}).\]
In particular,
$m_\lambda$ is even for every strict partition $\lambda$ of $n$ with
$\varepsilon(\lambda)=0$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Equivariance holds by construction, and $A^2=-\operatorname{Id}$ follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:eigenspinors}.

Let $\tau$ be the involution of $\Xi_n$ acting as $(-1)^q$ on $\Xi_{n,q}$. Then
\[\tau(\tilde\sigma \cdot \psi)=\operatorname{sign}(\sigma)\tilde\sigma\cdot\tau(\psi).\]
Thus, $\tau$ maps every irreducible $\hat\Sigma_n$-representation $W$ to $\operatorname{sign}\otimes W$. On the other hand, $\tau$ anticommutes with $D$, hence $A$, therefore interchanging $P^+$ and $P^-$.

If $\varepsilon(\lambda)=0$, the representation labelled $\lambda$ is
isomorphic to its own twist by the sign character, so it occurs as many times in $P^+$ as it does
in $P^+\otimes\operatorname{sign}$, forcing $m_\lambda$ to be even.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:mod4}
If $n\equiv1\pmod 4$, then $m_\lambda$ is even for every strict partition
$\lambda$ of $n$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
Consider the real element of the Clifford algebra
\[\omega=\prod_{i<j}\frac1{\sqrt2}(\alpha_{ij}-\alpha_{ji}).\]
Having fixed a tournament $\mathscr{T}$, examining the action of the individual factors shows that Clifford multiplication by $\omega$ maps $\psi_\mathscr{S}$ to $\pm\psi_{\mathscr{T}\setminus\mathscr{S}}$; in other words, $\omega$ realizes the isomorphism $*$ of Lemma~\ref{Pd}.

This isomorphism can be seen to be $\hat\Sigma_n$-equivariant as follows. Each factor $\alpha_{ij}-\alpha_{ji}$ of $\omega$ commutes with itself and anticommutes with $\alpha_{ij}+\alpha_{ji}$; since each of the remaining $N-1$ factors anticommutes with $\alpha_{ij}\pm\alpha_{ji}$, and $N-1$ is odd due to the assumption $n\equiv1\pmod 4$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
 \label{eqn:omegaalphaij}
\begin{aligned}
\omega\cdot (\alpha_{ij}-\alpha_{ji})&=-(\alpha_{ij}-\alpha_{ji})\cdot\omega,\\
\omega\cdot (\alpha_{ij}+\alpha_{ji})&=(\alpha_{ij}+\alpha_{ji})\cdot\omega.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Each $t_j$ is the product of $1+(n-2)$ elements of the form $\alpha_{ij}-\alpha_{ji}$, which anticommute with $\omega$, and $n-2$ elements that commute; since $1+(n-2)$ is even, $t_j$ commutes with $\omega$. Hence, $\omega$ acts in a $\hat\Sigma_n$-equivariant way.

Moreover, \eqref{eqn:omegaalphaij} implies $\omega\cdot\alpha_{ij}=\alpha_{ji}\cdot\omega$, hence
\[\omega\cdot \alpha_{ij}\cdot\alpha_{jl}\cdot\alpha_{li}
=\alpha_{ji}\cdot\alpha_{lj}\cdot\alpha_{il}\cdot\omega
=-\alpha_{ji}\cdot\alpha_{il}\cdot\alpha_{lj}\cdot\omega.
\]

This implies that $\omega$ anticommutes with $D$. Since $N$ is even,
$(-1)^q$ and $(-1)^{N-q}$ coincide and $\omega$ anticommutes with
$A$. Thus, $\omega$ interchanges the eigenspaces $P^+,P^-$ of
Corollary~\ref{cor:doubling}, and each irreducible representation
occurs with even multiplicity.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
